chunks: Critical nodes of a switch-mode supply. The question: What are some important nodes of consideration of switch mode power supplies? Why?
The critical nodes of a switching supply are where layout decides whether it works well. The input loop carries fast current pulses, so any inductance there causes voltage spikes.
The switch node swings the full input voltage in nanoseconds, so it pushes noise into nearby copper. The feedback node is sensitive, so it picks up that noise.
Ground carries both noisy and quiet currents.
Think of a house with a workshop and a nursery. The power saw and hammer (input loop and switch node) are loud and sudden.
The sleeping baby (the feedback pin) wakes at the smallest sound. The floor (ground) carries vibration from every room.
So the workshop goes at one end, the nursery at the other, and the shaking stays out from under the crib.
The nodes to study are VIN (with C in at the pins), SW (and the BOOT capacitor tied to it), GND, the divider tap FB, and the output.

The input and ground connections form the hot loop; the feedback wire from the divider to the FB pin is the sensitive path (drawn long here only for clarity; in layout the divider sits next to the FB pin so this trace is short).
High di/dt: current that changes very fast, as in the input (hot) loop. Through inductance it makes spikes ("Routing the buck input capacitor").
High dV/dt: voltage that changes very fast, as at the switch node. Through stray capacitance it pushes current into neighbors ("Routing the buck switch node").
Feedback pin: where the chip compares a scaled copy of the output with an internal reference. A tiny current there makes a big voltage.
PGND and AGND: the power ground (noisy) and the analog ground (quiet) ("Star grounding").
The switch node swings 12 volts in 3 nanoseconds. Say just 0. 1 picofarads of stray capacitance couples it to the feedback pin, which has 5 picofarads to ground.
The two capacitances split the step like a divider: 12 times 0. 1 over (0. 1 plus 5) about 0. 235 volts. Against a reference near 0. 8 volts, that is a big error.
So the feedback trace stays short and far away. That is the whole idea.
"I sort nodes by mechanism. The input hot loop (input cap and both switches) carries nanosecond pulses of the full load current, so its inductance causes overshoot and EMI.
The switch node swings the full input voltage, so it couples through capacitance and radiates; keep it short and small.
The feedback and compensation nodes are high impedance and pick up noise, so they stay short and away from the inductor.
Ground is shared between noisy power return and quiet reference, so I separate them, and the output path is about resistance."
